analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, sale, and possession of named semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on this bill; its assault-weapons provisions were folded into the broader 1994 crime bill, H.R. 4296, which passed and was signed into law, and 52 members had signed on as cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to manufacture, sell, or possess the semiautomatic assault weapons named in the bill or matching its definitions, and to transfer or possess ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It grandfathers guns people already legally own, exempts hundreds of named hunting and sporting firearms, and adds tougher penalties for using one of these weapons during a violent or drug-trafficking crime. The ban would have expired on its own after 10 years.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by gun violence, if the restrictions reduce access to the weapons and magazines singled out for use in mass and gang violence. Sponsors also point to police and the public facing fewer military-style firearms on the street.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to manufacture, transfer, or possess the semiautomatic assault weapons named in the bill — including Colt AR-15s, Intratec TEC-9s, Uzis, MAC-10s, and Kalashnikov copies — or any rifle, pistol, or shotgun meeting its two-feature definitions.
Prohibits transfer or possession of large-capacity ammunition feeding devices — magazines, belts, or drums holding more than 10 rounds — and treats those devices as firearms under federal law.
Adds enhanced federal penalties for using or possessing a semiautomatic assault weapon during a crime of violence or a drug-trafficking crime.
Requires new banned weapons and magazines to carry serial numbers showing they were made after the ban, and mandates a Form 4473 paper trail for assault-weapon purchases.

analysis.who_pays: Firearms manufacturers and importers lose the right to make or sell the named models; licensed dealers and buyers take on new Form 4473 recordkeeping duties with fines up to $1,000 and up to six months in jail for violations. People who already owned the banned guns keep them, but their resale is restricted.

drawbacks.text: The ban grandfathers every lawfully possessed weapon and exempts several hundred named hunting, sporting, and target firearms listed in Appendix A — so banned guns already in circulation stay legal, and makers of functionally similar firearms outside the banned features keep selling.
The ban was written to repeal itself after exactly 10 years, so the restriction was never permanent even if enacted.

The Attorney General's study of the ban's effect on violent and drug crime only begins 12 months after enactment, with a report due 30 months after — meaning the law would take effect with no evidence of its impact on crime in the record.
Gun owners and sellers bear real compliance costs: a Form 4473 for assault-weapon purchases, private-sale recordkeeping, and penalties of up to $1,000 and six months in prison for knowing violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The restrictions target a narrow, high-profile set of firearms and magazines while deliberately leaving the much larger hunting and sporting gun market untouched, which limits both the public-safety gain and the economic cost. The honest weaknesses are the grandfathering of existing weapons, the feature-based definition that similar firearms can be redesigned around, and the built-in 10-year sunset — so the bill trades breadth for political feasibility.

outcome.mechanism: The House never voted on this bill itself; it sat in the Judiciary Committee, and on May 5, 1994 the record pointed to H.R. 4296 — the omnibus 1994 crime bill — as the vehicle, where the assault-weapons language became law under this same title and took effect for 10 years before sunsetting in 2004.

narrative.text: Introduced November 17, 1993 by Rep. Chuck Schumer with 52 cosponsors, 51 of them Democrats and 1 a Republican.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, which held hearings in April 1994.
On May 5, 1994 the House action history points to H.R. 4296, the omnibus crime bill, as the vehicle for this legislation.
The bill text specified the ban would take effect on enactment and repeal itself 10 years later.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of the ban came out ahead: the restrictions took effect as part of the 1994 crime bill. Manufacturers of the hundreds of exempt hunting and sporting firearms, and existing owners of banned guns, were protected by the grandfathering and Appendix A carve-outs.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors; its provisions later moved into the omnibus crime bill he also championed.

for.name: Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Joined Schumer in introducing the bill.

for.name: 51 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Becerra, Cardin, Pelosi, Markey, Rangel, and Waxman.

for.name: Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Pushed the omnibus crime bill containing the assault-weapons ban through Congress and signed it into law in September 1994.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Campaigned hard against the assault-weapons ban and the crime bill carrying it, targeting members who voted for it.

against.name: Firearms manufacturers and importers of banned models
against.role: Colt, Intratec, Action Arms, and foreign makers named in the bill
against.what_they_did: Would have lost the legal right to make, import, or sell the named assault weapons and high-capacity magazines; opposed the ban.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 51 of the 52 cosponsors were Democrats, with just one Republican — and the fight over the ban in the final crime bill split largely, though not entirely, along party lines.

industries.note: The bill outlaws the manufacture, transfer, and possession of their named products — Colt AR-15s, Intratec TEC-9s, Uzi and Galil rifles, MAC-10s, Kalashnikov copies, and imported models like Norinco and Steyr AUG — plus magazines over 10 rounds. The industry's interest in keeping these products on the market ran directly against the bill's public-safety purpose.

Dealers take on new paperwork duties — a Form 4473 for every assault-weapon sale, retention requirements, and fines up to $1,000 and six months in jail for knowing violations — but the hundreds of hunting, sporting, and target firearms exempted in Appendix A remain sellable.
Several hundred named rifles and shotguns — Remington 700s, Ruger Mini-14s, Browning and Mossberg models — are explicitly exempted, shielding that market while competitors' tactical lines are banned.
